answer: Comparing programs that target different diseases requires a common unit of health. Simple counts, such as cases prevented, cannot be compared across heart disease, diabetes, and mental health interventions because they measure different outcomes. The quality-adjusted life year (QALY) and the disability-adjusted life year (DALY) solve this by combining length and quality of life into a single metric. A QALY weights each year of life by a quality factor from zero to one, allowing diverse programs to be expressed on the same scale and ranked by the health they produce.

faqs.q: What is a quality-adjusted life year (QALY)?
faqs.a: A QALY combines length of life and quality of life into one number, weighting each year lived by a quality factor between zero (death) and one (perfect health), so health gains from different programs can be compared.

faqs.q: Why can't programs be compared using simple counts like cases prevented?
faqs.a: Cases prevented measure different outcomes across diseases and ignore severity and duration, so they cannot be added or ranked across programs targeting heart disease, diabetes, and mental health.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a QALY and a DALY?
faqs.a: A QALY measures health gained, with higher values better, while a DALY measures health lost to disease and premature death, with lower values better. Both put diverse conditions on a common scale.
